name: Bursa
desc: Ottoman capital before Edirne and İstanbul, stacked on the north slope of Uludağ so every street either climbs or falls. The Hanlar district around Koza Han is still a working silk and textile market, with tea trays carried between mulberry trees in the courtyard. Eat İskender kebab where it was invented, then take the cable car out of the haze.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the basin traps haze in high summer and drizzle from December
tip: Koza Han's upstairs galleries are where the actual silk sellers work; the ground-floor cafés are for coach parties.
todo: Tea in the Koza Han courtyard
İskender kebab at a founding-family branch
Tophane clock tower and Osman's tomb
rev: Visitors rate the mosques, the silk hans and the food higher than they expected, then complain about traffic, concrete sprawl and how far apart the good bits are.
entry: Free to walk; mosques free, city museums ≈₺150 (≈€4)
onward: Bursa Yenişehir (YEI) is tiny; most arrive from İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) by road, or by fast ferry to Mudanya then 30 min to the centre

name: Grand Mosque of Bursa
desc: Twenty domes on twelve piers, paid for out of the ransom of a battle and finished in 1399. A fountain still runs under the open oculus in the middle of the prayer hall, and the walls carry 192 panels of monumental calligraphy painted straight onto plaster. It is dim, cool and unusually unfussy for an imperial mosque.
season: Year-round — coldest and emptiest on January mornings
tip: Come between prayers on a weekday and sit by the şadırvan; the calligraphy reads best from the side galleries under the oculus.
todo: The şadırvan fountain under the oculus
Read the 192 calligraphy panels
Walk straight out into Koza Han
rev: Almost everyone finds the fountain-inside-a-mosque arrangement startling and the atmosphere better than İstanbul's big mosques; the complaint is the shoe-rack scrum and tour groups talking over prayers.
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then 2.5 h by road, or the Mudanya fast ferry; it is in the middle of Bursa's pedestrian centre

name: Cumalıkızık
desc: A 700-year-old Ottoman village on Uludağ's skirt, cobbled roughly enough that you watch your feet, with some 270 timber-and-rubble houses in ochre and blue leaning over the lanes. Weekends bring busloads for village breakfast and mulberry juice; midweek mornings it is chickens, woodsmoke and women selling raspberries from doorsteps.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — raspberry season in June is when the stalls are best
tip: Go on a weekday before ten; on summer Sundays the lanes are a single-file queue and every courtyard has become a breakfast restaurant.
todo: Village breakfast in a courtyard
Mulberry and raspberry stalls
The ethnography house museum
rev: People love the lanes and the breakfast and then say it has been half-turned into a theme park by weekend crowds and identical souvenir stalls; the cobbles are genuinely hard on ankles.
onward: Bursa city, then the 22 bus or a 25-min taxi east to the village car park; no parking inside

name: Green Mosque and Green Tomb
desc: Mehmed I's mosque and tomb face each other across a lane on the slope above the city. The tomb is sheathed outside in turquoise tile and inside in cuerda seca panels so deep they look wet. The mosque hides a tiled sultan's loge above the entrance that most visitors walk under without ever looking up.
season: Year-round — spring light through the tomb's stained glass is the best of it
tip: Ask the caretaker about the hünkâr mahfili upstairs in the mosque; the finest tilework in Bursa is behind that small door.
todo: Cuerda seca mihrab in the tomb
The upstairs sultan's loge
Turkish and Islamic Arts Museum next door
rev: Consistently called the best tilework anyone sees outside Topkapı, with grumbles about the souvenir arcade crowding the tomb terrace and shifting opening hours at the museum.
entry: Free (mosque and tomb); museum in the medrese ≈₺100 (≈€3)
onward: Bursa city centre, then the T1 tram to Yeşil or a 10-min taxi uphill

name: Muradiye Complex
desc: Twelve small tombs in a walled garden of cypress and rose, holding the sultans, princes and mothers who lost Ottoman succession fights — including Cem Sultan, who died in Italian exile. Each türbe is different inside: painted vaults, İznik panels, bare whitewash. It is the quietest important place in Bursa and almost nobody is in it.
season: Apr–Jun for the garden, Oct for the plane leaves
tip: One caretaker unlocks the tombs in rotation with a big key ring; walk the loop slowly and point, and he will open whichever ones you ask for.
todo: Cem Sultan's painted tomb
Şehzade Mustafa's İznik panels
The 17th-century house museum on the corner
rev: Visitors describe it as the calmest hour they spent in Bursa; the recurring complaints are that several tombs stay locked and there is almost no English labelling.
onward: Bursa city centre, then a 15-min walk west from Ulu Cami or a short taxi

name: Uludağ
desc: The ancient Mysian Olympus, a 2,543 m limestone bulk that puts snow within sight of the Marmara. Winter is Turkey's oldest ski scene — hotels packed at the base, long lift queues, firs furred with hoar frost. In summer the meadows above the treeline fill with crocus and day walkers who came up on the cable car.
season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for walking — Apr–May and November are mud and closed lifts
tip: The Teleferik from Teferrüç in the city is the cheap way up and drops you at Sarıalan; the road via Kirazlıyayla charges a national-park fee per car and jams on winter weekends.
todo: Cable car from Teferrüç to Sarıalan
Walk to the Aras and Kilimli glacial lakes
Sledge hire at the Oteller Bölgesi
rev: Skiers call the terrain limited but the snow reliable and the prices low; everyone complains about weekend crowds, the cable car queue and hotels that feel like 1980s package blocks.
entry: National park vehicle fee ≈₺200 (≈€5) · cable car ≈₺600 (≈€14) return
onward: Bursa city, then the Teleferik from Teferrüç (35 min) or 33 km by the Kirazlıyayla road; İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) is 3 h away

name: İznik (Nicaea)
desc: Nicaea of the church councils, still boxed inside five kilometres of Roman and Byzantine wall with gates you drive straight through. The grid inside is low, green and slow, ending at a lake lined with fish restaurants. Working studios have brought back the quartz-bodied İznik tile that died out in the 1600s, and you can watch a kiln being loaded.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the lake plain is humid and still in August
tip: The Lefke Gate's triple arch and the Roman theatre are free and usually deserted; buy tiles only from a studio that fires its own kiln, not from the shops on the main street.
todo: Walk the Lefke and İstanbul gates
Ayasofya Mosque's council-church floor
A working tile studio kiln
rev: Travellers find the walls and the tile workshops rewarding and the town pleasantly unpolished, while noting the lakefront is scruffy and several monuments were shut for restoration for years.
entry: Town free; İznik Museum ≈₺150 (≈€4) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 2 h by road round the gulf; from Bursa it is 80 min by dolmuş via Orhangazi

name: Mudanya
desc: Bursa's Marmara port, and the town where the armistice ending the Turkish War of Independence was signed in a seafront house that is now a museum, furnished as it was in 1922. Behind the promenade the old quarter is Greek-era stone and timber, gently restored. The promenade itself is a kilometre of fish tables facing the sunset.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — August fills every table with Bursa weekenders
tip: The İstanbul fast ferry lands here rather than in Bursa; the connecting bus leaves from the terminal door and costs a fraction of the taxi everyone else takes.
todo: Mudanya Armistice House museum
Sunset fish on the promenade
The restored houses on Yalı Caddesi
rev: People like it as a low-key ferry town with good fish and a genuinely interesting museum; the common complaints are limited swimming, weekend traffic and a seafront that gets loud after dark.
onward: İstanbul Yenikapı fast ferry direct to Mudanya (about 2 h), then 30 min by bus to Bursa

name: Trilye (Zeytinbağı)
desc: A Byzantine-Greek olive village 12 km west of Mudanya, its stone houses with wooden oriels dropping in terraces to a small harbour. The Fatih Mosque was the 8th-century church of Hagios Stephanos and still shows the brickwork; the roofless Taş Mektep schoolhouse stands above the lanes. Everything smells of olive oil, fig and woodsmoke.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the November olive harvest is the moment to buy oil
tip: Come on a weekday: on summer weekends Bursa empties into the two harbour restaurants and parking on the single lane down is hopeless.
todo: Fatih Mosque, the old Hagios Stephanos
The Taş Mektep ruin above the lanes
Buy oil and olives at a village press
rev: Reviewers call it the prettiest thing on the south Marmara shore and then warn about weekend gridlock, restaurant prices that jumped once it was discovered, and steep unforgiving cobbles.
onward: İstanbul fast ferry to Mudanya, then 20 min west by dolmuş; from Bursa it is 45 min by car

name: Gölyazı
desc: An island village on Lake Uluabat joined to the shore by a causeway, built over ancient Apollonia — column drums do duty as doorsteps and a sarcophagus as a horse trough. Fishermen mend nets under a plane tree said to be 700 years old, and pelicans and herons work the reed beds a hundred metres off.
season: Mar–May for pelicans and blossom, Sep–Oct for still water
tip: A fisherman will take you out for an hour for the price of a modest lunch — arrange it at the causeway in the morning, not by phone.
todo: Ancient column drums reused in walls
Boat out to the pelican reeds
The ruined Greek church by the shore
rev: Photographers rave about the light and the storks; others report a village that is visibly poor and half-abandoned, with litter on the shoreline and very little to eat beyond one or two fish shacks.
onward: Bursa, then 40 km west on the İzmir road and a signposted turn at Uluabat; occasional dolmuş from Bursa's Nilüfer terminal

name: Troy
desc: Nine cities stacked in one mound above the Trojan plain, with the Bronze Age walls and the sloping ramp of Troy VI still standing well enough to read. Alone it is a confusing pile of old trenches; with the Troy Museum's rust-coloured cube down the road, the sequence finally makes sense. The wooden horse in the car park is a prop.
season: Apr–May and Sep–Oct — there is no shade on the mound in July and August
tip: Do the museum in Tevfikiye first, then the mound, and walk the boardwalk anticlockwise so the layers arrive in chronological order.
todo: The Troy VI wall and ramp
Troy Museum's gold and Polyxena frieze
Look out over the silted Trojan plain
rev: Half of visitors call it the most atmospheric heap of stones they have walked, the other half find it underwhelming without a guide; everyone agrees the museum rescues the visit.
entry: ≈€15 · Troy Museum ticketed separately ≈€12 · both covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Çanakkale (CKZ) has thin flight links; most come from İstanbul (IST) over the 1915 bridge, then 30 km south from Çanakkale by dolmuş or car

name: Gallipoli Battlefields
desc: Pine and scrub across 33,000 hectares of ridge above the Dardanelles, with trench lines, cemeteries and monuments left roughly where the fighting stopped in 1915. At Lone Pine and Chunuk Bair the opposing trenches are eight metres apart. The Turkish 57th Regiment memorial and the Anzac sites share one hillside and are visited very differently.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — 25 April is Anzac Day, when the peninsula is sealed and full
tip: Hire a car or a licensed guide from Eceabat instead of a coach tour out of Çanakkale; the sites are 40 km apart and the buses give you eight minutes at each.
todo: Lone Pine and Chunuk Bair trenches
The 57th Regiment memorial and cemetery
Kabatepe interpretation centre
rev: Visitors describe it as unexpectedly moving and beautifully kept, while warning that rushed group tours, loudspeaker commentary and midsummer heat can flatten the experience entirely.
onward: İstanbul (IST), 4 h by road to Eceabat via the 1915 bridge, or the Çanakkale–Eceabat car ferry across the strait

name: Anzac Cove
desc: A 600-metre shingle beach under crumbling ochre cliffs, where the landing of 25 April 1915 went wrong before breakfast. It is smaller than every photograph suggests — seven minutes to walk end to end — and the ground rises immediately into the gullies that decided the campaign. Ari Burnu cemetery sits on the headland at the north end.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Anzac Day itself needs a permit and a very early start
tip: Come at first light before the buses roll down from Beach Cemetery; the cove is a war grave, and swimming here is discouraged even though nobody stops you.
todo: Ari Burnu cemetery on the headland
Atatürk's 'Johnnies and Mehmets' inscription
Look up into the Sphinx and the gullies
rev: Almost everyone is struck by how tiny and hemmed-in the beach is; complaints centre on coach convoys, litter in high season and a road that has been eroding into the sea for years.
onward: Eceabat by ferry from Çanakkale, then 12 km north by car or tour minibus; no public bus goes to the cove

name: Assos (Behramkale)
desc: A Doric temple of Athena on a 230 m volcanic crag with Lesbos filling the horizon, and a stone village clinging to the slope below. Aristotle taught here for three years and married the ruler's niece. The old harbour at the bottom is a single row of stone buildings turned into small hotels, with water deep enough to swim straight off the rocks.
season: May–Jun and Sep — August fills the harbour hotels and the one road down
tip: Sleep at the harbour but see the temple at sunset from the top; the descent to the harbour is a 1-in-5 cobbled hairpin that punishes a loaded car.
todo: Temple of Athena at sunset
The Ottoman humpback bridge below the village
Swim off the harbour rocks
rev: The view and the swimming get near-universal praise; the standard gripes are cramped harbour rooms at Aegean prices, the brutal access road, and touts on the village lane.
entry: Acropolis ≈₺200 (≈€5) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İstanbul (IST) then 5 h by road, or Edremit Koca Seyit (EDO) 1 h away; the last 3 km down to the harbour is steep and narrow

name: Bozcaada
desc: Ancient Tenedos: a small island of vineyards, poppies and constant wind, with a Venetian-Genoese fortress guarding a harbour of Greek stone houses in faded blue and ochre. Ayazma and Sulubahçe face south into clear water. A dozen working wineries press Çavuş and Kuntra grapes grown in quantity almost nowhere else.
season: Jun and Sep — August is a booked-out crush and winter ferries cancel in northerlies
tip: Leave the car at Geyikli and rent a scooter; the island is 40 km² and the ferry vehicle queue in summer eats more time than the whole island takes to cross.
todo: Winery tasting in the old Greek quarter
Ayazma beach before nine
Walk the castle walls at sunset
rev: Repeat visitors love the wine, the cobbled quarter and the light; complaints are August prices, a ferry that strands people in bad weather, and a harbour that is now mostly boutique hotels.
onward: İstanbul (IST) then 5.5 h by road to Geyikli-Yükyeri iskele, and a 35-min ferry; foot passengers can also sail from Çanakkale in summer

name: Gökçeada (Imbros)
desc: Turkey's largest island, 90 minutes off Kabatepe, with abandoned Greek hill villages — Zeytinli, Tepeköy, Dereköy — that refill every August with returning families. It was the country's first cittaslow and runs largely on organic farming. Aydıncık's shallow salt lake is the windsurf spot; Kefalos and Laz Koyu are where you actually swim.
season: Jun and Sep — the meltem blows hard all August and ferries stop in winter storms
tip: The Greek villages sit 300 m up and are cold after dark even in August, and the last ferry back leaves early — day-tripping from Çanakkale is a wasted day.
todo: Tepeköy and Zeytinli stone villages
Kefalos bay swim
Marmaros waterfall in the hills
rev: Visitors praise the emptiness, the goat cheese and the wild coast, and warn that public transport is minimal, half the villages are ghost towns, and vehicle ferry places sell out weeks ahead in August.
onward: İstanbul (IST) then 4.5 h to Kabatepe pier via the 1915 bridge, and a 90-min ferry; there is a small seasonal airstrip

name: Adatepe and Yeşilyurt
desc: Two stone villages on the southern skirt of Kaz Dağları, rescued from collapse by architects and now the most self-consciously handsome places in the Troad. Adatepe has an olive-oil museum in the old mill and the Zeus Altar on the rock above, where the gods supposedly watched the Trojan War. Yeşilyurt is steeper, quieter and less restored.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the villages are cool when the coast below is not
tip: Climb to the Zeus Altar at first light: the whole Gulf of Edremit and Lesbos lift out of the haze, and by ten the minibuses arrive from Assos.
todo: Zeus Altar rock at sunrise
The olive oil museum in the old mill
Coffee in Adatepe's plane-tree square
rev: People find the stonework and the view genuinely lovely, then note that both villages have become boutique-hotel and gift-shop economies with almost no local life left outside the season.
onward: Edremit Koca Seyit (EDO) 45 min away, or İstanbul (IST) and 5 h by road; signposted off the Küçükkuyu–Ayvacık road

name: Kaz Dağları (Mount Ida)
desc: Homer's Ida, a 1,774 m ridge of endemic Kazdağı fir and black pine between the Troad and the Gulf of Edremit, cut by streams that stay cold through August. The Çanakkale side above Bayramiç is the quiet one: forest roads, plateau hamlets, and a summit view that takes in Bozcaada, Lesbos and the Trojan plain at once.
season: May–Jun for flowers and water, Sep–Oct for the ridge — snow on top Dec–Mar
tip: Approach from Bayramiç and Yassıçalı for empty forest roads; the popular southern waterfalls run a daily vehicle quota that is gone by mid-morning all summer.
todo: Ridge walk to Karataş summit
Endemic Kazdağı fir stands
Night sky from a plateau hamlet
rev: Walkers rate the forest and the water highly and grumble about unsigned trails, the quota system on the Edremit side, and mining and quarry disputes that have scarred parts of the range.
entry: Free on the Çanakkale forest roads; national park entry from the south ≈₺100 (≈€2.50)
onward: Edremit Koca Seyit (EDO) for the southern side, or Çanakkale and 70 km east to Bayramiç for the northern forest roads

name: Kilitbahir Castle
desc: Mehmed II's clover-leaf fortress on the European bank at the narrowest point of the Dardanelles, 1,200 m across from its twin in Çanakkale. The three-lobed keep is unlike anything else the Ottomans built, and from the tower you look straight down on tankers passing at what feels like walking distance. Reopened after years behind scaffolding.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the strait funnels wind hard in winter
tip: Take the small Çanakkale–Kilitbahir ferry rather than the Eceabat one; it lands at the castle gate and runs roughly hourly.
todo: Climb the clover-leaf keep
The hillside 'Dur yolcu' inscription
Watch shipping from the ramparts
rev: Visitors call the keep the most interesting castle interior on the strait and the ferry crossing half the pleasure; the complaints are steep unlit stairs and erratic winter opening hours.
onward: Çanakkale waterfront, then the small vehicle ferry across the strait (about 15 min) which lands beside the castle

name: 1915 Çanakkale Bridge
desc: The longest suspension span in the world, 2,023 m between red-and-white towers, jumping the Dardanelles between Lapseki and Gelibolu. The crossing takes four minutes and replaces a ferry queue that could run to three hours in August. The best view is not from the deck but from the shore roads below, where the towers stand clear of the strait.
season: Year-round — strong northerlies occasionally close it to high-sided vehicles
tip: The toll is HGS electronic only; confirm your hire car has a working transponder before you cross or the fine arrives by post weeks later.
todo: Cross at dusk with the towers lit
Shore-road viewpoint on the Lapseki side
Combine with Gallipoli on the Thrace side
rev: Drivers are unanimous that it turned a half-day ferry ordeal into a coffee break, while locals on both banks complain the ferry towns lost their trade and the toll is steep for a short hop.
entry: Toll ≈₺500 (≈€12) per car, HGS electronic only
onward: İstanbul (IST) then the O-6 and O-5 motorways across Thrace; this is the direct road from Europe to Troy and the northern Aegean

name: Selimiye Mosque
desc: Sinan's verdict on his own career, finished at 86: a single 31.2 m dome on eight piers, lifted so the interior is one uninterrupted volume of light. Four 70 m minarets carry three balconies each, and a muezzin's platform stands in the dead centre with a fountain running underneath it. It reads far larger inside than out.
season: Year-round — winter mornings give the emptiest interior
tip: Come half an hour before sunset prayer and sit under the central platform; the upside-down tulip carved into one of its marble bases is the detail everybody hunts for.
todo: The upside-down tulip under the mahfil
Arasta bazaar in the substructure
Dome from the courtyard at dusk
rev: Architects and casual visitors alike call it the finest Ottoman interior anywhere; complaints are restoration scaffolding that has come and gone for years and coach groups that arrive all at once at midday.
entry: Free (mosque); Foundation Museum in the medrese ≈₺100 (≈€3)
onward: İstanbul (IST), then 2.5 h by motorway bus to Edirne otogar and a short taxi; Edirne has no airport

name: Edirne
desc: Ottoman capital for ninety years and still built like one: three imperial mosques inside a kilometre, a covered bazaar by Sinan, and a plain west of town where three rivers meet under long Ottoman bridges. The food is its own argument — calf's liver fried paper-thin, and almond marzipan. Greece and Bulgaria are each twenty minutes away.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the Thracian plain is baking in July and grey in January
tip: Eat tava ciğeri somewhere that fries to order off Saraçlar Caddesi, then walk out over the Meriç bridge at dusk to the riverside beer gardens in Karaağaç.
todo: Üç Şerefeli Mosque's four different minarets
Tava ciğeri with fried peppers
Meriç bridge and Karaağaç at sunset
rev: Day-trippers from İstanbul consistently wish they had stayed the night; the usual complaints are a scruffy modern centre, aggressive bazaar hawkers and buses that dump you far from the monuments.
onward: İstanbul (IST), then 2.5 h on the O-3 motorway by bus; long-distance trains no longer run usefully to Edirne

name: Bayezid II Complex and Health Museum
desc: A 1488 hospital on the bank of the Tunca where the mental ward was treated with running water, scent and music — musicians played three days a week — three centuries before European asylums stopped using chains. The hexagonal domed ward is now a museum with slightly eerie mannequins, and the mosque, medrese and soup kitchen around it are intact.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the riverside floods and turns to mud after winter rain
tip: It is a 20-minute walk out past Sarayiçi or a cheap taxi, and it is run by Trakya University, so the Museum Pass Türkiye does not work here.
todo: The hexagonal music-therapy ward
The imaret and medrese courtyards
Walk back along the Tunca bridges
rev: Most people call it the most memorable museum in Thrace and the mannequin dioramas either charming or unintentionally funny; the complaints are the walk from town and thin English labelling.
entry: ≈₺200 (≈€5) — university-run, not on the Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: İstanbul (IST) then 2.5 h by bus to Edirne, then a taxi across the Tunca; walkable from the centre in half an hour

name: Kırkpınar Oil Wrestling and Sarayiçi
desc: On an island in the Tunca where the sultans kept their Edirne palace, two thousand men in leather kispet trousers pour olive oil over each other and wrestle for three days each summer — a contest running since 1362. Out of season it is meadow, storks, an empty stadium, and the surviving palace kitchens and Justice Pavilion in the grass.
season: Late Jun–early Jul for the festival; otherwise Apr–Oct for the ruins and the storks
tip: Festival week fills every bed in Edirne and across the Bulgarian border, so book two months out or take the early bus from İstanbul and return the same night.
todo: A morning round in the grass arena
Palace kitchens and Justice Pavilion ruins
Stork nests on the Tunca bridges
rev: Those who make it for the festival call it the strangest and best sporting event in Turkey; the standard warnings are brutal heat with no shade, packed stands and touts reselling seats.
onward: İstanbul (IST), 2.5 h by bus to Edirne, then 3 km north-west along the Tunca by taxi or on foot

name: Enez (Ainos)
desc: Ancient Ainos at the mouth of the Meriç, where Thrace runs out into Greece. A Genoese-Byzantine castle stands over the village with the roofless church of Hagia Sophia inside it, and below runs a dozen kilometres of empty Saros Gulf sand with water clean enough that the Aegean crowd would ruin it if they knew.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming — Saros water stays cold and clear later than the Aegean
tip: Drive past the castle to Sultaniçe or Erikli for the sand, and stop at the Gala Lake hides on the way back for pelicans, flamingos and spoonbills.
todo: Hagia Sophia ruin inside the castle
Sultaniçe beach at the river mouth
Gala Lake bird hides
rev: People are startled by how empty and clean the beaches are and by the scale of the castle; the complaints are almost no infrastructure, mosquitoes off the delta and a long drive from anywhere.
onward: İstanbul (IST) then 4 h by road via Keşan; buses reach Keşan and a dolmuş covers the last 24 km

name: İğneada Floodplain Forests
desc: Longoz: alder, ash and oak standing in seasonal freshwater between Black Sea dunes and the Strandja hills, one of very few floodplain forests left in Europe. Boardwalks run out over Mert and Erikli lakes, and in spring the water sits knee-deep among the trunks, loud with frogs and warblers. Bulgaria is seven kilometres north.
season: Apr–Jun for flooded forest and birds, Sep–Oct for colour — mosquitoes are serious Jul–Aug
tip: Bring repellent and boots, and use the Mert Lake boardwalk reached from the road south of İğneada village rather than the one by the main park sign.
todo: Mert Lake boardwalk at dawn
Dune ridge between forest and sea
Swim off the long empty beach
rev: Birders and photographers rate it very highly; others report mosquitoes in clouds, boardwalks in poor repair after winter, and a village with only a handful of basic pensions.
onward: İstanbul (IST), then 3.5 h by road via Vize and Demirköy; buses reach Kırklareli and a dolmuş covers the rest

name: Dupnisa Cave
desc: Three linked caves under the Strandja forest, some 3,200 m long, with a river in the lower gallery loud enough to drown conversation. Lit walkways pass columns, curtains and rimstone pools, and the temperature holds at about 13 °C all year. Five bat species winter here, which is why the cave shuts for half the year.
season: May–Sep only — closed to visitors through the bat hibernation months
tip: Take a fleece even in August, and confirm it is open before you drive: the last 12 km from Sarpdere is forest road and there is nothing else out there.
todo: The river gallery walkway
Kuru Mağara's column chamber
Bat roosts at the upper entrance
rev: Visitors call it far bigger and wetter than expected and the forest drive worth it alone; the complaints are slippery steps, patchy lighting and people arriving in winter to find the gate locked.
onward: İstanbul (IST), 3 h by road to Demirköy, then 12 km of forest road; no public transport goes to the cave

name: Kıyıköy
desc: A fishing village walled in by Byzantine ramparts on a headland between two river mouths on the Black Sea. Below the walls, the Aya Nikola monastery is carved entirely from the rock — nave, columns, baptistery, all of it — and usually empty. Small boats run up the Pabuçdere into forest that comes down to the waterline.
season: Jun–Sep — the sea here is cold, and Nov–Mar is grey, wet and largely shut
tip: The rock monastery sits at the end of a signposted path from the lower gate and is unlocked; go before the İstanbul day-trippers arrive around noon at weekends.
todo: Aya Nikola rock-cut monastery
Boat up the Pabuçdere river
Walk the Byzantine gate and walls
rev: Weekenders like the monastery and the river trips and the cheap fish; the recurring complaints are basic pensions, litter on the beach in August and a sea too cold for many.
onward: İstanbul (IST), 2.5 h by road via Saray; dolmuş from Vize a few times a day

name: Yıldız Mountains (Strandja)
desc: A low, wet, oak-and-beech massif along the Bulgarian border — the last stand of Euro-Siberian forest in Turkey, and empty in a way nothing else within three hours of İstanbul is. Villages like Sarpdere, Balaban and Armutveren are timber-framed with vine porches and one tea house. The roads are single-track, unsigned and slow.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter fog and mud make the forest roads miserable
tip: There is almost no fuel between Demirköy and Kırklareli, so fill up before you turn off, and download the map because there is no phone signal in the valleys.
todo: Drive the Demirköy–Sarpdere forest road
Timber-porch villages and their tea houses
Look for black storks over the valleys
rev: Those who go describe genuine emptiness and good forest; the honest warnings are that there is nothing to eat, nowhere to stay outside Demirköy, and logging trucks own the roads on weekdays.
onward: İstanbul (IST), then 2.5 h to Kırklareli and north on the Demirköy road; a car is essential

name: Vize
desc: A Thracian hill town with a Roman theatre excavated below the citadel and a 6th-century church, Little Hagia Sophia, still standing under its original dome and now used as a mosque. Bronze Age dolmens and burial mounds sit in the fields around. Almost nobody stops on the way to the Black Sea, which is the whole appeal.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is windy and bleak in winter
tip: The theatre is behind the municipality building and unfenced; if the church door is locked, ask at the tea house on the square and somebody will fetch the key.
todo: Little Hagia Sophia's original dome
The Roman theatre below the citadel
Thracian dolmens in the fields
rev: Visitors are surprised by how intact the church is and how deserted the theatre feels; the complaints are erratic opening, no signage in any language and nowhere decent to eat.
onward: İstanbul (IST), 2 h by road on the Saray highway; regular buses from Kırklareli and İstanbul Esenler

name: Tekirdağ
desc: A Marmara port town known for two things: köfte bound with rice and cumin, and rakı distilled here since the 1930s. The Rákóczi House is a Hungarian prince's exile home turned museum, restored down to the panelling and furnished by Budapest. The seafront promenade runs for kilometres and fills every summer evening with families.
season: May–Jun and Sep — August is hot, crowded and the sea inside the bay is not the cleanest
tip: Eat the köfte at a charcoal grill near the old bazaar; the motorway service-station versions trading on the name are a different and much worse food.
todo: Tekirdağ köfte over charcoal
Rákóczi House museum
Sunset on the seafront promenade
rev: People come for the köfte and leave content, while noting the town itself is largely concrete, the beaches are poor and the port dominates the view.
onward: İstanbul (IST) or Çorlu (TEQ), then 1.5 h by the coastal road or motorway; frequent buses from İstanbul Esenler

name: Şarköy and the Ganos Hills
desc: The Ganos ridge drops straight into the Marmara here, and the slope between is one of Turkey's oldest continuous vineyard belts — Thracian, then Byzantine, then Greek, and now a dozen small wineries that will pour for you without an appointment. Şarköy itself is a plain beach town; the reason to come is the road and the vines above it.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — harvest is September, and August is a domestic-holiday crush
tip: Drive the ridge road from Mürefte to Uçmakdere rather than the coast road, and stop at Hoşköy for the small producers who still sell by the demijohn.
todo: Taste at a Mürefte or Hoşköy winery
The ridge road above the vineyards
Grilled fish at Hoşköy harbour
rev: Wine travellers rate the producers well above the region's reputation; the complaints are that Şarköy's own seafront is over-built, the beaches are average and several wineries close on Mondays.
onward: İstanbul (IST) or Çorlu (TEQ), then 2.5 h by road via Tekirdağ; a car is the only sensible way to reach the vineyards

name: Uçmakdere
desc: A single-track road falls 700 m off the Ganos escarpment in a run of hairpins to a fishing hamlet with one grocery and a stone jetty. Paragliders launch from the top most weekends because the sea breeze funnels reliably up the slope. Cyclists climb it as a test piece, and the view down the Marmara from halfway is the payoff.
season: May–Oct — the road is greasy and sometimes blocked by rockfall after winter rain
tip: Go down in low gear and be back up before dusk: there is no lighting, no barrier, and nowhere for a large vehicle to turn around.
todo: Watch the paraglider launch on the ridge
Coffee at the hamlet jetty
Swim off the shingle below the road
rev: Paraglider pilots and cyclists call it one of the best descents near İstanbul; drivers report a genuinely frightening road surface and locals complain that weekend traffic now blocks the hamlet.
onward: İstanbul (IST), 2 h to Tekirdağ then west on the coastal road; the turn-off is signposted between Kumbağ and Mürefte

name: Yalova Termal
desc: Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman baths in a wooded valley 12 km up from the Marmara shore, fed by water that has come out at 55–60 °C for two thousand years. The lead-domed Kurşunlu bath is the one to use; the 1930s republican buildings around it are period pieces in cracked marble. Plane trees keep the valley several degrees below the coast.
season: Oct–Apr — the point of a hot bath is not August
tip: Buy a session at the historic Kurşunlu rather than a hotel spa, and go midweek; on Sundays the valley is one long day-trip queue from İstanbul.
todo: Session in the Kurşunlu bath
Atatürk's Walking Mansion in the park
Walk up the valley to the springs
rev: Regulars swear by the water and the setting; complaints are tired changing rooms, weekend crowding and modern hotel spas charging resort prices for the same source.
onward: İstanbul Yenikapı–Yalova fast ferry (about 75 min), then a 20-min dolmuş up the valley from Yalova terminal

name: Karaca Arboretum
desc: A private arboretum on a hillside above Yalova, begun by one collector in 1980 and now holding thousands of taxa, with the country's largest collection of grafted weeping and cut-leaf forms. It is laid out as a garden rather than a plantation — ponds, a Japanese section, and maples and liquidambars that turn hard in November.
season: Apr–May for magnolia and blossom, late Oct–Nov for maple colour
tip: It closes on Mondays and shuts early in winter; the November colour week is the best of the year and almost nobody outside Turkish plant circles knows about it.
todo: Grafted weeping-form collection
The pond and Japanese section
November maple colour
rev: Gardeners call it world-class for the size of the site and the labelling unusually good for Turkey; the complaints are the steep paths, limited shade and no café worth the name.
onward: İstanbul Yenikapı–Yalova fast ferry, then 10 km south-west by taxi towards Samanlı; signposted from the Termal road

name: Çınarcık and the Yalova Coast
desc: The stretch of Marmara shore west of Yalova where İstanbul keeps its summer houses: pebble coves, pine slopes dropping to the road, and a promenade of tea gardens. The Erikli and Delmece plateaus rise straight behind, with waterfalls in the beech forest and ten degrees of relief. The water is cleaner here than anywhere on the inner Marmara.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming — July and August weekends multiply the population
tip: Skip the town beach and drive west past Koru for the coves, then take the forest road up to Delmece Yaylası where it is cold enough to want a jumper in August.
todo: Coves west of Koru
Delmece plateau forest road
Erikli waterfall walk
rev: Weekenders like the water and the quick ferry hop; the complaints are ranks of holiday blocks along the shore, a shortage of parking and jellyfish in some Augusts.
onward: İstanbul Yenikapı–Yalova fast ferry, then 20 min west by dolmuş; by road it is 2 h round the gulf from İstanbul

name: Lake Sapanca
desc: A 45 km² freshwater lake between two forested ridges, an hour from İstanbul on the motorway, ringed by walnut and cherry orchards and a great many weekend hotels. The southern shore road is the quiet side; the northern one carries the traffic. Morning mist lifting off the water with the ridges behind it is what everyone comes to photograph.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — autumn colour on the ridges is the best of it
tip: The lake is a drinking-water reservoir, so swimming is banned and actually enforced; hire a pedalo or walk the southern shore path instead of arriving in a swimsuit.
todo: Southern shore walk at first light
Cherry and walnut stalls in season
Kırkpınar village tea gardens
rev: İstanbullus love it as the nearest green weekend and warn each other about Friday-evening traffic, hotel prices that double at weekends, and the disappointment of learning you cannot swim.
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 1 h on the O-4 motorway; or the high-speed train to Arifiye and a 10-min taxi

name: Taraklı
desc: Some two hundred Ottoman timber houses in a steep valley, whitewashed with dark beams and jettied upper floors, saved before the concrete arrived and now a cittaslow. The Yunus Paşa mosque of 1517 has a wooden interior and the hamam still works. Wooden spoons, the town's old trade, are still turned in workshops on the main street.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — it snows properly here in winter, which is beautiful and very cold
tip: Stay a night in one of the restored konaks: the day-trip crowd is gone by five, and the lit lanes after dark are the entire reason to come.
todo: Sleep in a restored timber konak
The working hamam of 1517
Watch a spoon-turner at the lathe
rev: Visitors call it the most convincingly intact Ottoman town near İstanbul; the complaints are that half the houses are still derelict, there is little to do after dusk, and weekend day-trippers fill the two cafés.
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 2 h by road via Geyve; buses from Sakarya (Adapazarı) run several times a day

name: Justinian's Bridge (Sangarius Bridge)
desc: Justinian's 430 m bridge over what used to be the Sakarya, built in the 560s to carry the imperial road east. The river moved centuries ago, so seven enormous arches now stride across dry farmland and a stream, with the stub of a triumphal arch at one end. You can walk the whole deck without meeting anyone.
season: Year-round — spring greens the fields, winter turns the approach track to mud
tip: It is signed as Beşköprü off the Adapazarı–Kaynarca road; come at low sun so the arches throw shadows across the fields, and walk the full length rather than shooting it from the roadside.
todo: Walk the full 430 m deck
The triumphal arch stub at the east end
Photograph the arches at low sun
rev: Everyone who finds it is astonished it is not famous and equally astonished at the litter, the grazing sheep on the deck and the total absence of any information board.
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 1.5 h on the O-4 to Adapazarı, then 8 km south-west on the Kaynarca road

name: Acarlar Floodplain Forest
desc: The largest alder floodplain forest in Turkey, some 1,500 hectares of trees standing in shallow black water behind the Black Sea dunes near Karasu. Flat-bottomed boats and a boardwalk get you in among the trunks, where herons, cormorants and otters work the channels. Ten kilometres north the Sakarya meets the sea across a wide grey beach almost nobody uses.
season: Apr–Jun for high water and birds — Nov–Mar is wet, grey and mostly shut
tip: Boat trips leave from the Karapınar side and only run when enough people turn up, so ring ahead or go on a weekend morning.
todo: Punt among the flooded alders
Boardwalk at dawn for herons
Sakarya river mouth beach
rev: Birdwatchers rate the forest highly and everybody complains about mosquitoes, unreliable boat departures and the industrial port creeping along the coast nearby.
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 2 h by road via Adapazarı to Karasu; the longoz is signposted from the Kaynarca road

name: Kartepe
desc: A 1,600 m ridge above Lake Sapanca with the most reliable snow within an hour of İstanbul: a handful of lifts, one long blue running down into beech forest, and a view north over the Gulf of İzmit. It is a day-trip mountain rather than an alpine resort. In summer the summit road becomes a picnic and paraglider spot.
season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for the summit road — April and May are mud
tip: Drive up before nine at weekends or the access road jams solid; lift tickets sell out and the car park fills long before the queues form.
todo: Ski the long forest blue
Summit view over the Gulf of İzmit
Snowshoe walk in the beech woods
rev: Skiers call it convenient rather than good — short runs, thin snow in mild winters — while the summit view and the drive up get consistent praise.
entry: Road/park entry ≈₺150 (≈€4) per car · day lift pass ≈₺900 (≈€21)
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 1 h on the O-4 to Kartepe, then 20 km of switchbacks; shuttles run from Sapanca in season

name: Maşukiye
desc: A stream village on the northern skirt of Kartepe where restaurants build platforms out over the water and grill trout on them. Above the houses the road climbs through beech to the Suadiye waterfall and the plateaus. It is unashamedly a weekend eating destination and entirely worth it if you turn up on a Tuesday.
season: May–Oct for the streamside tables — the beech colour in late October is the best week
tip: Prices roughly double at the places nearest the main junction; drive two kilometres further up the valley for the same trout at half the money.
todo: Trout on a platform over the stream
Walk up to Suadiye waterfall
Continue to the Kartepe summit road
rev: Families love the setting and the noise of the water; the standard complaints are tourist-trap pricing, near-identical restaurants and a valley road gridlocked on summer Sundays.
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 1 h on the O-4 then 10 km south from Kartepe; dolmuş from İzmit runs hourly

name: Kerpe
desc: Sandstone cliffs eroded into overhangs, arches and stacks on the Black Sea coast north of Kandıra, with a small harbour and a beach at the foot of them. The water is cold and unusually clear for this coast, and the rock turns orange in late light. Kerpe, Kefken and Cebeci run in a line, each with its own cove.
season: Jun–Sep — swell shuts the beaches for days at a time and winter is bleak
tip: Cebeci and Sarısu are quieter than Kerpe itself, and the currents at the river mouths are genuinely dangerous — they drown people most summers.
todo: Walk the eroded cliffs at sunset
Boat out to Kefken island
Fish lunch at the harbour
rev: Weekenders praise the rock formations and cheap fish, and complain about litter after August, rough pension standards and a sea that is too cold and too rough half the summer.
entry: Free; some beaches charge ≈₺100 (≈€2.50) for a sunbed
onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW), 1.5 h by road via Kandıra; dolmuş from İzmit via Kandıra in summer

name: Söğüt
desc: The winter pasture where Ertuğrul Gazi settled and where his son Osman began an empire, which is why the tomb here — rebuilt by Abdülhamid II — draws a state-backed ceremony every September with hundreds of costumed riders. The town itself is a quiet Bilecik market place with a small ethnography museum and not much else.
season: September for the Ertuğrul commemorations; otherwise Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
tip: The tomb takes fifteen minutes, so drive on up to the ridge above town where busts of seventy-two Turkic rulers stand in a row — faintly absurd and completely photogenic.
todo: Ertuğrul Gazi's tomb and garden
The ridge line of Turkic ruler busts
Söğüt ethnography museum
rev: Turkish visitors find it moving and foreign visitors often find it thin — a rebuilt 19th-century tomb rather than anything medieval — and September brings crowds the small town cannot absorb.
onward: İstanbul (SAW) or Ankara (ESB) then the high-speed train to Bilecik or Bozüyük, and 30 min by road to Söğüt

name: Osmaneli
desc: A Sakarya-valley town of Greek and Armenian merchant houses in stone and timber, a good number of them restored, one of them a hamam that still runs. The old quarter climbs from the river to the shell of the Hagios Georgios church, and the whole circuit takes an hour. The Ankara–İstanbul high-speed line stops here, which is a strange privilege for a town this size.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the valley is humid and heavy in July and August
tip: The high-speed train from İstanbul or Ankara puts you ten minutes' walk from the old town, which makes this the easiest car-free day trip in the whole region.
todo: The restored merchant house street
Hagios Georgios church shell
Bath in the working hamam
rev: Rail travellers are pleasantly surprised by the streetscape and the quiet; the complaints are that restoration is patchy, the church is usually locked and there is almost nowhere to eat properly.
onward: High-speed train from İstanbul Söğütlüçeşme or Ankara direct to Osmaneli station, then a 10-min walk uphill

name: Bilecik and the Şeyh Edebali Tomb
desc: The tomb of Osman's father-in-law and teacher stands on a bluff above the Belkoz gorge with a modern complex around it and two hundred metres of cliff below. Down in the old quarter, the Orhan Gazi Mosque of 1331 is among the oldest Ottoman buildings still standing — small, square and completely plain, which is the point.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is cold, windy and often foggy in winter
tip: Walk down from the tomb terrace into the old quarter instead of driving; the stepped lane past the Orhan Gazi Mosque is the only part of Bilecik that still looks Ottoman.
todo: Gorge view from the tomb terrace
Orhan Gazi Mosque of 1331
The stepped lane through the old quarter
rev: Pilgrims and history travellers find the site well kept and the view genuinely dramatic; others say the modern complex has smothered the tomb and the rest of the town is unremarkable concrete.
onward: High-speed train from İstanbul or Ankara to Bilecik station, then a short taxi up to the tomb terrace

name: Marmara Island
desc: The Proconnesus of antiquity, source of the white-and-grey veined marble in half the Byzantine buildings of İstanbul. The quarries still work, and there are abandoned faces above Saraylar you can walk straight into. Beaches at Çınarlı and Asmalı, an interior of bare hills and dry-stone walls, and a fraction of Avşa's crowds.
season: Jun–Sep — ferries thin out from October and cancel outright in bad weather
tip: Saraylar's open-air marble museum, a field of ancient sarcophagi and column drums beside the harbour, is free and empty; the island bus meets the ferry and runs about three times a day.
todo: Saraylar open-air marble museum
Swim at Çınarlı or Asmalı
Walk into an abandoned quarry face
rev: Visitors like the quiet and the strange marble landscape, and warn that quarry dust and lorries dominate Saraylar, accommodation is basic, and getting between villages without a scooter is slow.
onward: İstanbul Yenikapı fast ferry (about 4 h with island stops), or shorter crossings from Tekirdağ and Erdek

name: Avşa Island
desc: The Marmara's holiday island: two long sandy beaches, vineyards that still supply a drinkable local wine, and a summer population that multiplies roughly twentyfold. In June and September it is a pleasant, slightly shabby seaside town with clean water and cheap fish. In August it is a ferry queue set to loud music.
season: June and September — August is chaos and winter has almost no sailings
tip: Stay on the Yiğitler side rather than Türkeli if you want to sleep, and buy the return ferry ticket the day you arrive, because Sunday sailings sell out.
todo: Swim at Altınkum in the early morning
Local wine from a village producer
Boat trip round to Ekinlik island
rev: Turkish holidaymakers come back every year for the sand and the price; the constant complaints are August noise, overbooked pensions, litter on the main beach and brutal Sunday ferry queues.
onward: İstanbul Yenikapı fast ferry (about 3 h) or the shorter crossing from Tekirdağ; the island is walkable and scooters are for hire at the pier

name: Erdek
desc: A Marmara resort at the neck of the Kapıdağ peninsula, with a plane-shaded promenade, a working fishing harbour and small islands offshore twenty minutes away by boat. Turkish families have come here for generations, the fish restaurants are cheap by Aegean standards, and the sunsets look straight down the gulf towards Bandırma.
season: Jun–Sep — half-shut and grey from November to March
tip: Take the day boat out to Zeytinli or Fener island rather than swimming from the town beach, which is crowded and not the best water on the peninsula.
todo: Day boat to the offshore islands
Fish supper on the promenade
Sunset from the harbour mole
rev: Regulars praise the value and the boat trips; the recurring complaints are jellyfish in some Augusts, a town beach that gets murky, and holiday-block sprawl along the shore road.
onward: İstanbul, then the fast ferry to Bandırma (about 2 h) and 20 min by dolmuş to Erdek

name: Kapıdağ Peninsula
desc: An island tied to the mainland by two sandbars, a thousand metres high in the middle and forested with chestnut and pine, ringed by a road that passes coves most drivers never stop at. Ocaklar and Narlı face west into the sunset; the northern side towards Ilhanköy is cliffs and empty water. From the ridge the Marmara looks like a lake.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct for the loop drive, Jul–Aug for swimming
tip: Drive the loop anticlockwise from Erdek so the sea stays on your right, and take the unsigned tracks down to the north-coast coves, which have no facilities and almost nobody on them.
todo: Loop the peninsula road in a day
A north-coast cove with no facilities
Chestnut forest on the ridge road
rev: Drivers and cyclists rate the loop and the empty north side highly; the warnings are potholed sections, no fuel outside Erdek, and coves that need a high car or a walk down.
onward: İstanbul, fast ferry to Bandırma, then 20 min to Erdek where the peninsula road starts; a car or scooter is essential

name: Cyzicus
desc: One of the great cities of the Propontis, whose Temple of Hadrian Byzantine writers ranked among the wonders of the world. What is left is a field of tumbled marble, a vast amphitheatre split down the middle by a stream, and stretches of wall lost in the maquis. It is unfenced, unlabelled, usually deserted, and only recently back under excavation.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — by midsummer the site is chest-high in thistle
tip: The amphitheatre is the piece worth finding, signposted off the Erdek road near Hamamlı; wear long trousers and boots because of the thorns and the ticks.
todo: The stream-split amphitheatre
Temple of Hadrian marble field
Trace the city wall through the scrub
rev: Ruin hunters find the scale astonishing and the solitude complete; everyone else reports no signage, no path, no shade and a real risk of walking past the main monument without noticing it.
onward: İstanbul, fast ferry to Bandırma, then 15 km north on the Erdek road; the turnings are poorly signed, so use a map pin

name: Bird Paradise National Park (Lake Manyas)
desc: A shallow lake on the migration corridor between Europe and Africa, where some 260 species have been recorded and Dalmatian pelicans breed in flooded willows. A short boardwalk leads to an observation tower above the colony. The park is small and the lake's health has swung with agricultural runoff, so set expectations before you arrive.
season: Mar–May and Sep–Oct for migration — the pelicans are on nests from March
tip: Bring your own binoculars, because the tower stands 200 m off the colony and the park lends none; early morning before the wind gets up is the only worthwhile hour.
todo: Pelican colony from the tower
Boardwalk through the willow scrub
Visitor centre bird collection
rev: Birders say the spring passage is genuinely good; the widespread complaints are a tiny walkable area, a tower too far from the birds, and water quality that has visibly declined.
onward: İstanbul, fast ferry to Bandırma (about 2 h) then 20 min by road; Balıkesir Koca Seyit (EDO) is 1.5 h to the south
